chapter_theme: Heedlessness, especially the forgetting that comes with joy and success, is more dangerous than rage. To keep in mind what one has resolved is the skill on which everything else depends, and it is an inward fort or an inward leak.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the fault of heedlessness (531-532), what it brings on those who have it (533-535), the distinction of heedfulness (536-537), what to do with it (538), and how to attain it (539-540).

531.reading: The slackness that comes of the elation of great joy is worse than excessive anger.
531.nuance: A surprising ranking, because joy isn't usually the danger. சோர்வு is a letting go, and it comes when things go well. Parimelazhagar's reason is exact: anger sometimes at least kills an enemy, while this kills only oneself.

532.reading: Heedlessness kills fame as unremitting poverty kills understanding.
532.nuance: The comparison is the striking claim. நிச்ச நிரப்பு is not poverty but chronic poverty, and Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar make it daily begging to fill the stomach. Understanding is treated as something that material conditions can destroy.

533.reading: The heedless have no fame: that is the settled view of writers of every kind in the world.
533.nuance: The Kural rarely appeals to an all-schools consensus. Parimelazhagar explains why it can: every aim of life fails when one is heedless, so the claim isn't limited to polity.

534.reading: The fearful have no fortress; likewise the heedless have no good.
534.nuance: A fort is useless to one whose fear is inside it: the verse places the failure in the mind, not in the walls. So the heedless may have resources, and they do them no good.

535.reading: One who slipped by not guarding beforehand will later, when struck, grieve over his own error.
535.nuance: Regret is presented as the penalty. தன்பிழை matters: there is no one else to blame. Parimelazhagar adds that the things that could have been guarded against are enemies' moves, made by watching for such lapses.

536.reading: If not slipping, with anyone, at any time, is had without fail, nothing equals it.
536.nuance: Three universals. Parimelazhagar assigns each: toward all people, in good times and bad, in every matter. The condition வாயின் concedes how seldom this is met. Manakkudavar takes it as not making errors in giving justice, a narrower sense.

537.reading: Nothing fails to be done on the ground of being hard, if done with the tool of unforgetting care.
537.nuance: Attention is called a கருவி, a tool. Parimelazhagar notes that it is an inner instrument, the mind, set beside the external means of 483.

538.reading: What has been praised must be carefully done; those who slight it and don't do it have nothing through seven births.

positions.position: What is praised is what polity texts prescribe to kings, and lapsing means hell, as with neglect of caste duty.
positions.quote: நீதி நூலுடையார் இவை அரசர்க்கு உரியன என்று உயர்த்துக் கூறிய செயல்களைக் கடைப்பிடித்துச் செய்க;

positions.position: What is praised is virtue, as praised by the exalted, and the verse is about not neglecting it.
They are one's duties, and neglect means no rise in life. He doesn't mention births.

539.reading: When swollen with one's own joy, think of those who were ruined by negligence.
539.nuance: A practical remedy: history is used deliberately against one's own mood, at the moment it is hardest to think of it. Parimelazhagar notes that negligence and ruin arise together.

positions.position: The memory is a corrective to mood: thinking 'we too would fall that way' stops one exulting.
positions.quote: கெட்டாரை உள்ளவே, 'நாமும் அவ்வாறே கெடுதும்' என்று அதன்கண் மைந்துறார் என்பது கருத்து

positions.position: It leads to a specific precaution: a king should have what he eats, wears and smears checked, because past kings died that way.
positions.quote: இஃது உண்பவை, உடுப்பவை, பூசுபவை சோதித்துக் கொள்க என்றது.

540.reading: To gain what one has thought of is easy, if one can keep thinking of what one has thought of.
540.nuance: The verse is built on repetition of உள்ளியது, which enacts its own lesson. Parimelazhagar catches the particle மன்: it hints what remains unsaid, that this is just what people can't do. So 'easy' is an ironic word. It is easy only in the way the conditional describes.

links.note: 305 says anger kills the one who has it. In Parimelazhagar's argument for 531, anger at least sometimes reaches the enemy, while elated forgetting only kills oneself. The Aram book's worst self-destroyer gets demoted.
In Parimelazhagar's reasoning on 408, poverty doesn't ruin the good. 532 makes chronic poverty the very image of what destroys understanding. Either understanding survives poverty, or it doesn't.

421 builds an inner fort of understanding. 534 shows an outer fort falling to inner fear. Together they say that a fortress is finally a state of mind, which is unusual in a Porul section that counts forts as a limb of the state.

'Nothing is hard' appears with different conditions: 462 counsel, 472 knowing strength, 483 means and time, and here attention. The refrain's repetition suggests that no single one suffices, and each chapter has claimed the last word.
Same structure: what one has in mind is attained, if. 666's condition is firmness and 540's is continued remembering. They might be one quality seen from the will and from attention.

source_issues: 535: The Manakkudavar entry is marked [#] and is nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's, so I did not treat it as independent.
